lead: The moment-area method reads slope and deflection straight off the M/EI diagram, with no integration of equations. The area under M/EI between two sections gives the change in slope between them. The first moment of that area about one section gives how far the other section sits from the tangent drawn at the first. Engineers use it to check a cantilever or a simply supported beam quickly, and examiners use it because it tests whether you understand curvature rather than algebra.
prereq: You need: 5.1 for curvature M/EI, and Unit 3 for bending moment diagrams.

blocks.text: Draw the bending moment diagram, divide every ordinate by EI, and plot M/EI along the beam. Some syllabi call the results Mohr's theorems; others call the whole procedure the area-moment method.
θ_B − θ_A = area of M/EI between A and B
blocks.where: θ_A, θ_B are slopes in radians at sections A and B; the area is measured in (1/m) × m = radians.

blocks.text: t_B/A = first moment of that area about B
blocks.where: t_B/A is the vertical distance of B from the tangent drawn at A, in metres; the moment is area × horizontal distance of its centroid from B.

blocks.text: Sign rule: take sagging moment as positive, so a sagging beam curves concave upward (it sags downward). Plot M/EI on the sagging side as positive. Then t_B/A is positive when B lies above the tangent drawn at A. Keep one sign convention for the whole problem.

Theorem 1 gives only a change of slope, so you still need one known slope. Theorem 2 gives a distance from a tangent, not a deflection: the tangent at A may itself be tilted. The deflection of B is t_B/A only when the tangent at A is horizontal, as at a fixed end or at the centre of a symmetrically loaded span.

items: Draw the bending moment diagram for the beam.
Divide the ordinates by EI to get the M/EI diagram; split it into triangles, rectangles and parabolas if EI or the load changes.
Area of M/EI between two sections gives the change in slope.
Take the first moment of that area about the section whose deviation you want.
Use a known slope or known horizontal tangent to convert a deviation into a real slope or deflection.

sections.h3: Why area gives angle and moment gives deviation

blocks.text: Curvature is 1/R = M/EI. Take a slice of length dx. The two faces of the slice turn relative to each other by dθ = (M/EI) dx. Adding these small turns from A to B gives the total change in slope, which is Theorem 1.

For deviation, a turn dθ in a slice at distance x from B moves B by x dθ relative to the tangent to that slice. Adding x dθ over the whole length from A to B gives the deviation of B from the tangent at A. That sum is exactly the first moment of the M/EI area about B, which is Theorem 2.

The method is strongest where the M/EI diagram is simple shapes. A cantilever with an end load gives a triangle. A simply supported beam with a uniformly distributed load w over span L gives a parabola; the slope at a support is wL³/(24EI) and the central deflection is 5wL⁴/(384EI). For several loads, draw the moment diagram by parts: one triangle per point load, one parabola for the distributed load, and take areas and centroids shape by shape.

sections.h3: Worked pattern: cantilever with an end load

blocks.text: Take a cantilever fixed at A and free at B, length L, with a point load P at B. The moment at a section distance x from A is M = P(L − x), so M/EI is a straight line: PL/EI at the fixed end, zero at the free end.

Area of the triangle = ½ L (PL/EI) = PL²/(2EI). That is the slope at B, since the slope at A is zero. The centroid of a triangle with its base at the fixed end lies L/3 from A, so its distance from B is 2L/3. Then t_B/A = (PL²/2EI)(2L/3) = PL³/(3EI). The tangent at the fixed end is horizontal, so this deviation is the free-end deflection.
Numbers from the figure: L = 3 m, P = 8 kN, EI = 4000 kN·m², giving 0.009 rad and 18 mm as solved below.

figure.caption: The M/EI diagram for a 3 m cantilever with an 8 kN end load is a triangle, 0.006 m⁻¹ at the fixed end and zero at the free end. Its area gives the free-end slope and its moment about the free end gives the deflection.

spec.aria: A plot shows a triangular M/EI diagram for a cantilever with an end load, largest at the fixed end and zero at the free end.

examples.question: A cantilever of length 3 m carries a point load of 8 kN at its free end. EI = 4000 kN·m². Find the free-end deflection and slope by the moment-area method.
steps: Bending moment at the fixed end A: M = PL = 8 kN × 3 m = 24 kN·m. At the free end B it is zero.
M/EI at A = 24/4000 = 0.006 m⁻¹. At B it is zero, so the M/EI diagram is a triangle of base 3 m and height 0.006 m⁻¹.
Theorem 1: θ_B − θ_A = area = ½ × 3 m × 0.006 m⁻¹ = 0.009 rad. The fixed end has θ_A = 0, so θ_B = 0.009 rad.
The centroid of the triangle is L/3 = 1 m from A, hence 2 m from B.
The tangent at the fixed end A is horizontal, so the deflection of B equals t_B/A = 0.018 m = 18 mm, downward.
examples.answer: Slope at the free end = 0.009 rad; free-end deflection = 0.018 m = 18 mm downward.

delta = theta*(2*L/3)

traps: Reporting t_B/A as the deflection when the tangent at A is tilted; at a free end or an interior point the tangent is not horizontal, so you must add or subtract the tangent's own rise.
Forgetting that Theorem 1 gives only a change of slope. You need one known slope, usually zero at a fixed end or at the centre of a symmetric span.
Mixing units: M in kN·m and EI in kN·m² give M/EI in 1/m, area in radians and moment of area in metres. Convert to mm only at the end.
Taking the centroid distance from the wrong end. For t_B/A the lever arm is measured from B, not from A.
Using the full span L in the lever arm when the M/EI diagram is asymmetric. Split it into shapes and sum each area times its own centroid distance.

quiz.a: θ_B − θ_A = area of the M/EI diagram between A and B; t_B/A = first moment of that area about B, where t_B/A is the vertical distance of B from the tangent at A.

quiz.q: Why is the M/EI diagram divided by EI before taking areas?
quiz.a: Curvature is M/EI, and curvature integrated over length gives angle. The area of M alone would have units kN·m², not radians.

quiz.q: Why is t_B/A not always the deflection of B?
quiz.a: t_B/A measures from the tangent at A. If that tangent is tilted, B's true deflection includes the tangent's own rise over the horizontal distance.

quiz.q: A cantilever 2 m long carries 5 kN at the free end; EI = 2000 kN·m². Find the free-end slope and deflection.
quiz.a: M_max = 10 kN·m; M/EI = 0.005 m⁻¹; slope = ½ × 2 × 0.005 = 0.005 rad; lever arm = 4/3 m; deflection = 0.005 × 4/3 = 0.00667 m = 6.67 mm.

quiz.q: A simply supported beam of span 4 m carries a UDL of 6 kN/m; EI = 8000 kN·m². Find the slope at a support and the central deflection.
The M/EI diagram of a beam is a triangle of height h and base L. What do its area and moment about the apex end give?
quiz.a: Area ½Lh gives the change in slope between the ends. The moment about the apex end, using centroid distance 2L/3 from the apex, equals ½Lh × 2L/3 = L²h/3 and gives the deviation of the apex end from the tangent drawn at the taller end. The moment about the taller end uses L/3 and gives the deviation of the taller end from the tangent at the apex.

quiz.q: For a fixed-ended beam, why can the moment-area method give the fixed-end moments without integrating?
quiz.a: Both end slopes are zero and both end deviations from the opposite tangents are zero. Writing area = 0 and moment of area = 0 supplies two conditions that fix the redundant end moments.

beyond: Not for the exam. The same area-and-moment idea becomes the influence-line method for moving loads on bridges, where you need the largest deflection at any position of a truck. For beams with changing sections, or with cracks, the M/EI diagram is piecewise and the method still works shape by shape. Modern codes use numerical stiffness methods, but the moment-area check is still the fastest way to catch a wrong computer answer. Search next for non-prismatic beams and the Müller-Breslau principle.
